stem: A client develops sudden severe flank pain that comes in waves and radiates toward the groin. Urinalysis shows hematuria. The client has no fever or dysuria. Which condition is most consistent with these findings?

options.A: A ureteral stone causing renal colic

rationale: NIDDK identifies kidney/urinary stones as a cause of sharp pain in the back, side, lower abdomen, or groin and hematuria; stone pain may come and go in waves. A stone lodged in the urinary tract can obstruct urine flow and produce severe pain or bleeding, so A best fits the presentation. B can cause back/side/groin pain and bloody urine, but kidney infection more typically includes fever/chills and urinary symptoms such as frequent or painful urination, which are absent here. C commonly causes dysuria, urinary frequency/urgency and lower-abdominal discomfort rather than classic colicky flank-to-groin pain. D may cause back pain but does not explain hematuria or the urinary-tract radiation pattern.
educational_objective: Recognize renal/ureteral calculi by episodic severe flank pain radiating toward the groin with hematuria, and distinguish this pattern from urinary infection and musculoskeletal pain.
source_organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NIH
source_document_title: Symptoms & Causes of Kidney Stones; Definition & Facts for Kidney Stones; Symptoms & Causes of Kidney Infection (Pyelonephritis); Symptoms & Causes of Bladder Infection in Adults
source_version_date: NIDDK kidney-stone content last reviewed 2017; bladder-infection content last reviewed 2024; current NIH pages accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Symptoms & Causes of Kidney Stones > symptoms: sharp pain in back/side/lower abdomen/groin, hematuria, pain may come and go in waves. Definition & Facts > a stone that becomes stuck can obstruct urine flow and cause severe pain or bleeding. Kidney Infection > symptoms: fever/chills, frequent or painful urination, back/side/groin pain. Bladder Infection > symptoms: dysuria, urinary frequency/urgency and lower-abdominal discomfort.
source_claim_supported: Colicky flank pain radiating toward the groin with hematuria is strongly consistent with urinary stone disease, while fever/dysuria would favor infection and musculoskeletal pain does not explain hematuria.
